# Purpose and assumptions

This 60-minute session follows a separate 30-minute lecture. It consolidates
research computing foundations; do not add statistical-model explanations.
The previous 90-minute Day 3 materials remain reference, not an additional
90-minute obligation. The instructor must select the separate lecture's content.
Approximately 30 graduate students have received Ninya Quibod's introductory
R instruction. Documented exposure does not establish mastery.

Assume participants can access a prepared RStudio session (browser or already
installed Desktop). Confirm this before class; do not spend the hour installing
software. The supplied R script uses only base R. The required report
walkthrough also needs Quarto and knitr in the prepared RStudio environment.
Confirm these before class; participants should not install them during class. English materials match the existing AFEC course.

# Evidence from previous teaching

The [planning assessment](coverage-assessment.md) records the source review made
before authoring. All 30 PDF pages, corresponding PPTX text/notes and the complete
R script in `nina/` were inspected. No previous exercise datasets or student
responses are present, so completion and mastery remain unknown.

| Category | Previous coverage | Decision and reason |
|---|---|---|
| A: exposure suggests familiarity | pp. 8–13 arithmetic, assignment, naming/case; script comments, c(), sum(), mean(), help | Briefly reuse assignment and case in an import; omit calculator drills and memorization. Check rather than assume fluency. |
| A: exposure suggests familiarity | pp. 25–26 installations/plots; script hist(), boxplot(), ggplot() on diver respiration vs experience | Supply one familiar histogram; no package or plot-construction lesson. |
| B: likely conceptual ambiguity | pp. 14–15 Console vs Source and reopen exercises | Separate saved instructions, execution and live objects. Console checks are legitimate; scripts preserve the intended sequence. |
| B: likely conceptual ambiguity | p. 19 getwd/setwd and advice to put files in the same location; script absolute Windows paths | Use separate data/ and R/ folders; resolve one relative path from the Project. Folder browsing, opening a script and changing the working directory are distinct actions. |
| B: likely conceptual ambiguity | pp. 16–18 lists of types and structures, Harry Potter examples | Connect numeric/character/logical to column vectors and the whole table. One coercion example reveals why appearance alone is insufficient. |
| B: likely conceptual ambiguity | pp. 20–24 import, NA, inspection and factor conversion; script DIVER.csv -> diver and new respiration_log column | Explain file vs object, rows vs columns, one observation's meaning and missing vs observed values. Interpret outputs instead of repeating a function catalogue. |
| C: essential and not found | Project workflow, a worked absolute/relative comparison, class(), file extensions, Markdown/Quarto, fresh-session workflow | Introduce a prepared Project and class(); read QMD text and R code together, render it and show the HTML. |

A/B/C are planning judgments, not labels for students. Read the code and outputs
together, explaining each step as it appears. Participants may run the supplied
lines alongside the instructor. Do not add prediction questions, pair discussion
or independent tasks. Use questions from participants to adjust the pace.

## Precision when reinforcing previous explanations

Clarify these points without turning the class into a correction of another
instructor. Files need not be in a single flat folder. R can read formats other
than CSV. Console history may persist, but a saved script is the deliberate
record. head()/tail() default to six rows, `$` selects a column and levels()
reports factor levels. read_excel() is in readxl, not dplyr. Whole-number values
need not use R's integer storage (`30` versus `30L`). Most of these details are
for answering questions, not additional slides.

# Timing: 60 minutes including questions

| Minutes | Slides / activity | Emphasis |
|---|---|---|
| 0–6 | 1–3: SSD to RAM, folder tree and extensions | File vs object; relative paths need a starting point. |
| 6–25 | 4–7: absolute/relative paths, prepared Project, Save/Run, CSV import | Live IDE demonstration; connect Source -> Console -> Environment. |
| 25–45 | 8–12: types/structures, actual table, columns, NA, inspection | Read real output; one seedling per row; type and structure differ. |
| 45–55 | 13: script walkthrough | 2 min location, 3 import, 2 column/NA, 3 histogram. |
| 55–58 | 14: Quarto report | Read the QMD, click Render, open the HTML. |
| 58–60 | 15: recap and questions | Trace the whole route; retain buffer. |

Quarto is required. Keep its three-minute slot even if setup is delayed; shorten
the live restart or coercion example instead. The here example is optional and
appears only in the handout. If an R problem persists beyond two minutes, follow
the saved outputs together. If Render fails, use the saved report HTML while
explaining the QMD-to-HTML steps; record the problem for follow-up.

These are teaching allocations, not measured learner completion times. The
script is short and supplied in full, but a fresh participant rehearsal is
needed to establish the pace of the 15-minute walkthrough.

# Demonstration instructions

## Before class

Build with `make day3-2`; distribute only `dist/afec-day3-2-materials.zip`.
The ZIP contains the participant Project and self-contained slides/exercise/
report HTML, not this note, its answers or the planning assessment. The original
all-days ZIP and website do not automatically include this extra session.

Extract a fresh copy of the participant ZIP, preferably to a folder with a space
in its name. Open its `.Rproj` in the intended RStudio environment. Confirm its
Project name and `file.exists("data/seedlings.csv")`. Keep workspace
restore/save disabled; the supplied Project already requests this. Test opening
the script, running selected lines, seeing the histogram and reading local HTML.
Browser RStudio paths refer to the server, so demonstrate upload/extract/open if
that is how students will receive the folder. Desktop and browser menus can vary.
Check actual access for all participants separately from local validation.

## Files, panes and Projects

Show the Project root and its data/ and R/ subfolders. Explain absolute paths
from a drive/filesystem root, then relative paths from R's starting folder.
Opening the supplied Project establishes that folder; the script uses relative
paths. Do not teach getwd()/setwd() commands or personal absolute paths.
If input is missing, reopen the correct Project and check the folder structure.

Open the supplied script. Run its location section first, then the import.
Show the new object in Environment. Point to its Source line and the resulting
Console output. Save a harmless comment change to show saving does not execute
code. Use an isolated example `diameter <- c(2.1, 3.4, 4.7)` for a live Save/Run
comparison, then run the supplied script's import and column section to replace
that object with the real column.

If useful and time permits, restart R once and show that opening a script has
not recreated `seedlings`. Rerun from the top. Do not quit a participant's unrelated
session or use rm(list=ls()). Preserve the Project starting context and folder
structure so the relative paths resolve consistently.

## Optional here example and path comparison

Use the walkthrough's three-minute location allocation to explain the path
comparison too: personal absolute paths change with the
parent location; internal relative paths survive moving the whole Project.
No manual working-directory change is required. If demonstrating here, use
its i_am declaration at the top of the supplied script in a fresh participant
Project session. Confirm its generated path ends in data/seedlings.csv and the
two imports are identical. Do not add the optional here code to the core script
or require participant installation. here returns an absolute path constructed
from a portable specification; this differs from hard-coding a personal path.

## Table, column and missingness

Use the eight fictional seedling records. Species labels are placeholders, not
real taxa. One row follows one seedling over one interval. Stem diameter is in
mm, not adult DBH. A data frame's ordinary columns have different types but
matching lengths. Mention its list structure in one sentence only; no list
indexing exercise. class() identifies class; str() gives the wider picture.

Show `class(c(2.1, "unmeasured"))` once: numeric-looking text cannot be used as a
measurement without appropriate interpretation. A numeric column can contain
NA. Do not teach conversion workflows or silently replace a missing observation.
The survival column is logical because the CSV uses TRUE/FALSE/NA and read.csv
recognizes these values. Other import functions/values can produce different
types: inspect rather than assume.

The fourth diameter is missing, and the fifth survival status is unknown.
The histogram omits one missing diameter and shows seven measurements. Unknown
survival is not a known death. Do not add imputation, hypothesis testing or a
statistical-model exercise.

## Practical answers and expectations

See the instructor version of [the exercise](exercise.html#instructor-interpretation).
Participants receive `exercise.html` renamed from the solution-free build.
Expected results: data.frame, 8 x 4; character ID/species, numeric diameter,
logical survival; diameter length 8; histogram counts 0, 3, 3, 1.
The wrong starting folder R/ resolves data/seedlings.csv to R/data/seedlings.csv.
Moving the whole Project preserves its internal relative path. Editing an R
object does not rewrite the CSV; outputs need a deliberate export/render step.

# Required Quarto report walkthrough

Open `report.qmd` at the participant Project root; point to prose and the import
chunk, then Render. Default knitr execution starts from the QMD's directory,
which here is also the participant Project root. It imports its own data; it
must not rely on objects created interactively. The outer exercise/slides use
course authoring paths; students do not need to know that machinery.

Markdown supplies the document's plain-text structure; Quarto executes code and
renders the HTML. Do not teach YAML, chunk options or Markdown syntax. If the
runtime unexpectedly lacks Quarto/knitr, show the prepared `report.html`,
explain the rendering steps and record the environment issue for follow-up.

# Deliberate exclusions

No statistical inference, model fitting, package installation/updating, loops,
custom functions, matrix operations, factor internals, complex indexing, list
manipulation, Git, shell commands or general R syntax course. Reproducibility
here means preserving inputs and instructions and rerunning in a known context;
software versions and backups deserve one closing reminder, not a new tooling
lesson. A Project does not pin packages or guarantee reproducibility by itself.
